Still open: the session transcript also carries `ownerAccountUuid` and `ownerOrganizationUuid` fields in its `bridge-session` entries. That goes on the list for the owner to read before anything is pushed.

### 9:06 PM, the statistical bisect finds a bug that fails about a third of the time

This is milestone 3 on the real refund agent with the scripted model. `tests/planted.py` built 40 commits with a lookup bug at suspect 27: a `raise` sits inside a loop over a set of strings, and a set iterates in a different order in each Python process, so the lookup gives up on about one run in three.

- `whodunit lineup` named suspect 27, `Accept order ids written with a # or leading zeros`, at 95.2% after 48 replays across 11 of the 40 commits.
- It put the failure rate at 39% from that commit on and 1% before it. The true rate is about 33%.
- A scan from the oldest suspect would have had to work through 27 commits, each replayed often enough to catch a one in three failure.
- Replay time was 35 minutes, about 44 seconds per replay, on a machine with a load average near 70. The same replay takes 3 to 5 seconds on a quiet machine.

Then the rest of the pipeline on the same case:

- The brief took three tries to get right, and the first two are the interesting part. Both named the right commit and the right symptom and cited real spans, and both got the mechanism wrong: one blamed `lstrip`, the other said the `raise` was outside the loop, which would make it fail every time. Every sentence passed the citation check. So the check keeps a brief tied to the evidence and does nothing to stop a wrong reading of the diff. What fixed it was giving the model the changed code as it reads after the commit, with line numbers and indentation, and the measured failure rates with an instruction to explain why the failure is intermittent. The third brief has the loop, the set order and the 39%.
- Ruling: revert, given on the command line for this throwaway repo. No ruling has been recorded in this repo, because that is the owner's to give.
- Fix: the revert was committed on a local branch and replayed 8 times with no failures, which puts it at 95.8% fixed. The case was kept as a regression test.
- The case file page rendered from the record. A screenshot and the record are in `evidence/`.

Also added: `whodunit onset`, which reads the agent's ordinary runs from neatroots and brackets the failure between a good and a bad ref using the same change-point model, and `eval/score.py`, which scores cases against an answer key and refuses to run if the key's SHA-256 does not match the one committed beforehand.

A real-model case is running now. Dropping the ownership rule from the system prompt in the name of friendlier replies made the gateway's small model refund another customer's order in 3 runs of 8, so that prompt change is planted at suspect 31 of 40 and the statistical bisect is looking for it.

### 9:18 PM, a real prompt regression found on a real model, then patched

This is the case the project is for. In a planted history of 40 commits, suspect 31 is `Make the agent's replies friendlier`. It rewrites the system prompt and, along the way, drops the rule that an order must belong to the customer. Nothing errors. The gateway's small model simply refunds another customer's order some of the time.

- `whodunit lineup` named suspect 31 at 95.5% after 32 replays across 9 of the 40 commits, in 15 minutes of replay time. It put the failure rate at 57% from that commit on and 2% before it.
- The replays cost about 10 cents on the gateway.
- The brief was right on the first try this time. It quotes the dropped rule, points at the span where the model notes the order belongs to `cust_7` and refunds it anyway, and at the passing run where the same mismatch stopped the refund.
- Ruling: patch, given on the command line for this throwaway repo.
- The patch was written by the gateway's larger model. It kept "friendly" and "be warm" and put the ownership rule back. 0 failures in 6 replays, 98.2% likely fixed. Fewer replays were needed than for the lookup bug because this one fails more often.

The record and a screenshot of the case file are in `evidence/`.

Two fixes came out of this run. A reworded prompt was being classed as an agent-code change, because the diff only touches the string lines and the name `SYSTEM` sits in the context. And the damages step was counting every run of the workflow, including ones from before the culprit existed. It now counts ordinary runs on the culprit and later commits, and says so when there are none, as there are none here.

What this case still lacks is a motive. The history is planted, so no coding session asked for friendlier replies. That needs the second session.

## Sunday 11 October

### 12:29 AM, the victim has a real history

A second coding session grew `victims/refund-agent` while this one stayed out of git. It never edited the agent itself. For each change it called `eval/ask.sh`, which starts a fresh headless coding session with one ordinary request, so every commit has its own Entire checkpoint with the request that led to it.

- 55 commits to the agent in all: 2 sent from this session to test the mechanics, and 53 from the second session. Seven more requests made no commit and were dropped or reworded.
- 5 cases were sealed in `cases/`. Two fail every time and three fail some of the time, by the second session's own probes on the gateway model. The ranges hold 11 to 15 suspects each.
- The answer key is in `eval/answer-key.json`, which git ignores and this session has not opened. Its SHA-256, `d5b98bb3...4dca`, was committed as 4c45f7f before Whodunit ran on any case, and the file on disk matches it.
- `whodunit motive` shows the exact request behind the two test commits, so the motive step now has real material.

What it cost, as the second session reported it: about $18.40 for the 60 coding sessions, about $5 for the second session itself, and its estimate of $2 or less for about 480 probe runs on the gateway. That is roughly $25, which is more than the $10 to $15 this session guessed beforehand.

One thing to fix was found on the first test commit: the headless session added a co-author trailer naming its model. `eval/ask.sh` now turns that off and strips any that slip through.

The judging criteria were read from the public hackathon page and added to `AGENTS.md`. Two things stand out. cfo.ai is required and nothing exists for it yet. And neatroots, where most of the tracing work has gone, is not named on the page, so the evidence needs to show up in neatlogs cloud.

### 1:06 AM, the sealed eval: five planted regressions, none wrongly accused

Whodunit ran on the five sealed cases with replays on the gateway's small model. The answer key stayed unopened until every case had run. `eval/sealed/README.md` has the table.

- With 120 replays allowed per case: 3 of 5 solved, 0 wrong accusations, 2 where nobody was named.
- The two open cases were resumed from their own replays with more allowed, and both were then named correctly at 168 replays each. So 5 of 5 in the end, still with no wrong accusation.
- The two slow ones are the bugs that fail least often, about 12% and 14% of the time. On one of them the top suspect at 120 replays was the wrong commit, at 53%, and Whodunit named nobody.
- Replay spend was about $1.91 for all five cases.
- The ranges are short, 11 to 15 suspects, so this says little about savings against a scan on a long history.

For the first time the cases have motives. Three of them, in the words that were typed:

- `turned-away`: "one more for friendlier replies. When someone asks for a refund on an order that's still shipped and hasn't arrived yet, the agent is a bit blunt about it."
- `strangers-paid`: "since we capped the loop at 3 model calls, simple refunds feel slow, and most customers already tell us the order number and the amount."
- `cents-off`: "our new payments provider only accepts refund amounts in whole currency units".

Things that went wrong, and what was done:

- 6 of the 53 new commits carry an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer that Entire cannot resolve. Its log shows "condensation failed: failed to get commit object: object not found" for those sessions, and `entire doctor` finds nothing to repair. One of the six is the culprit of `half-done-batch`, so that case has no recorded request. Whodunit now says so and falls back to the commit's own message.
- Replays that ran side by side on one commit with one input could not be matched to their runs in neatroots, so one brief was first written without a failing run to look at. Each replay now carries its own tag in the trace, and the brief step makes a few tagged replays when it has no matched failing run.
- Three prompt changes were classed as agent-code, because the prompt is now a list called `SYSTEM_RULES`. Fixed.
- Two model-written briefs were overwritten with the no-model template during testing and had to be written again. That brings the count of model-written briefs and patches to 12, against a guideline of about 10 before Sunday 4:30 PM.
- Session transcripts are full of absolute paths, and those were landing in the case records. The motive step now strips them.

Not done: no ruling has been given for any of the five, because that is the owner's question to answer. The culprits fall into three kinds: prompt (`strangers-paid`, `wrong-order-refunded`), tool code (`cents-off`), and model settings (`half-done-batch`). `turned-away` is classed as agent code and reads like a prompt change, which is one more thing the classifier gets wrong.

    def __init__(self, eval_cmd: list[str] | None = None):

               "--repeats", str(req.repeats), "--commit", req.sha, "--run-id", req.run_id]

def worktree(repo: Path, sha: str, root: str | None = None) -> Iterator[Path]:
    """Detached worktree at sha in a temp dir; always removed and pruned, even on error."""
    tmp = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="agentbisect-wt-", dir=root))

                       capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
        yield path
    finally:

**An autonomous pit crew for AI agents.** Point Pitstop at an agent repo. It runs
the agent's evals, reads the neatlogs traces of the failing runs, works out the
root cause, patches the code, re-runs the evals, and keeps the patch only if the
numbers improve. Each accepted fix lands as its own git commit with before/after
metrics and trace ids. Patches that don't help are reverted.

Built for [neatHack](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon) (Oct 10–12, 2026) by team **4'feetus**.

**First real run** ([report](reports/pitstop-1010-2320-db0d.md)): Scout on `claude-haiku`, Pitstop on `claude-sonnet-4.6`, via the hackathon LiteLLM proxy.

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| tasks passing | 0/6 | **6/6** |
| tokens (6 tasks) | 58,879 | **16,302 (-72%)** |
| est. cost per eval run | $0.0697 | **$0.0251 (-64%)** |
| avg latency | 4.6 s | 3.2 s |

Three rounds, three accepted fixes, each its own commit with the evidence that justified it:

1. **Fenced JSON.** Every neatlogs trace ended in `scout.research status=ERROR JSONDecodeError`; the timelines showed answers starting with a markdown code fence. Pitstop stripped fences before parsing (+19 checks).
2. **Context bloat.** `people_search` returned ~50k chars of full profiles into context. Pitstop trimmed it to name/title (0 → 5 tasks pass).
3. **Invented numbers.** The prompt said "never leave a field null", so the model filled zerodha.com's missing funding with 0. Pitstop allowed null for unknown values (5 → 6).

Pitstop spent $0.21 (7 model calls), read 9 neatlogs traces back and ran 7 Entire Graph searches.

## How it works

```
            ┌──────────── evals (pitstop.toml: eval_cmd) ─────────────┐
            ▼                                                          │
  target agent ──traces──▶ neatlogs ──trace API──▶ evidence ─┬▶ DIAGNOSE (claude-sonnet-4.6)
  target repo ──entire graph search──▶ candidate fix sites ───┘
                                                                       │ ranked root-cause hypotheses
                                                                       ▼
            keep + commit ◀── ACCEPT ◀── compare ◀── evals ◀── tests ◀── PATCH (search/replace edits)
            revert        ◀── REJECT ◀──┘                     │
                                     repair once ◀── edit didn't apply / tests failed
```

1. **Evaluate.** Run the target's eval command (declared in its `pitstop.toml`).
   The harness meters every model call itself, so the agent can't hide steps.
2. **Collect evidence.** For each failing task: failed checks, a step-by-step
   timeline (tool calls, arguments, result sizes, errors, tokens per step) and
   the neatlogs spans and detections for that task's trace, read back through the neatlogs trace API.
3. **Localize.** Each failure signal (an exception, a failing tool call, an
   oversized tool result, an invented value) becomes an `entire graph search`
   over the target repo. Only hits in editable files are kept, as candidate fix sites.
4. **Diagnose.** The model returns ranked hypotheses, each citing evidence
   (task, step, failure text), and sees every earlier attempt and why it was rejected.
5. **Patch.** Minimal search/replace edits, limited to files the target marks
   `editable`. Evals and data are read-only, so the agent can't game its own tests.
   If an edit doesn't apply or the unit tests fail, the error goes back to the
   model for one repair attempt.
6. **Verify.** Re-run the evals. Accept only if more tasks pass, or more checks
   pass, or results stay equal with ≥10% fewer tokens, and no passing task
   regresses. Otherwise revert.
7. **Report.** A markdown + JSON report with the before/after table, every
   accepted diff, every rejected attempt and why, and all trace ids.

Pitstop has a hard USD budget (`--budget`) for its own model calls and stops
cleanly (reverting any half-applied patch) when it hits it.

# Suture

An agent that fixes broken agents, and only hands the fix over once an outside check shows it worked.

Built for neatHack, track "Build an agent that works (literally)".

neatlogs finds what broke and can suggest a fix. Suture tests the fix, and only hands it over once a signed outside check shows it worked.

## What it does

You point Suture at an AI agent that sometimes gets things wrong. Suture then:

1. Runs the outside check (StressProof, 12 probes) on the agent and saves the signed "before" report.
2. Reads the failing runs from the agent's neatlogs traces, so it fixes what actually broke, not what it guesses broke.
3. Asks the model for a patch and applies it to a copy of the agent, never the original.
4. Runs the agent's own tests, plus a new test written from the failure that fails on the original code.
5. Puts the patched copy online and runs StressProof again for the signed "after" report.
6. Keeps the fix only if quiet failures (wrong answers that look fine) are 0 and the score did not drop. Otherwise it throws the patch away and tries again, up to 3 times.
7. If a fix is kept, it opens a pull request. It never merges. A person decides.

## One run you can check

Target: Clerk, a small refund-lookup agent (`targets/clerk`). Its first draft answered broken requests with a confident, made-up answer.

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| StressProof score | 75 (PARTIAL) | 92 in the pull request, 100 in the latest re-run |
| Quiet failures | 1 | 0 |
| Attempts used | | 1 of 3 |
| Cost of the fix | | about $0.11 (model about $0.10, two outside checks $0.01) |

The signed reports and the numbers are in `evidence/`. The pull request is [#1](https://github.com/Sireadell/suture/pull/1).

## Try it yourself in one minute

```powershell
python -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
pip install -r requirements.txt
copy .env.example .env      # then fill in your own keys
python -m pytest targets\clerk
python -m suture.loop
```

Open any signed report link in `evidence/scorecard.json`. Each one is a StressProof page anyone can verify.

## How it uses the three event tools

| Tool | Use in Suture |
|---|---|
| neatlogs | Suture traces itself and the target agent. It reads failing runs and its own cost back through the neatlogs command line. |
| Entire | Build sessions are recorded as checkpoints on this repo, linked from the submission. |
| cfo.ai | The business plan: price per accepted fix, cost per fix, revenue and runway. Numbers come from the real run above. |

## What existed before the event

StressProof, the outside checker, is my earlier project (github.com/Sireadell/stressproof). Suture calls it as a service. Everything in this repo (the repair loop, the neatlogs reading, the keep rule, Clerk and the other test agents) was written during the event.

## What this is not

- It does not merge anything. It opens a pull request and stops.
- It does not promise a fix every time. If it cannot prove a fix, it hands back nothing and says so.
- It is not a general bug fixer. It repairs one kind of fault, agents that answer bad input with a confident wrong answer.
- It does not prove the target is perfect. A score of 100 means the 12 probes passed, nothing more.
- Today it has one fully proven target. More are in `targets/` and are not claimed until their runs are in `evidence/`.

- neatlogs Fixes is not used yet. The command line has no Fixes command, and connecting GitHub in neatlogs did not work for this project.
- The neatlogs login I have is read-only, so Suture cannot write its verdict back into neatlogs.
- neatlogs cost counts leave out the model's thinking tokens, so Suture also keeps its own counters and reports the larger number.

from __future__ import annotations

import json

import neatlogs

from rootline.clients.entire import graph_search
from rootline.clients.external import call_external
from rootline.clients.git import git
from rootline.clients.llm import complete, parse_json, read_prompt


def _candidates(state: dict) -> list[dict]:
    detect = state["outputs"]["DETECT"]
    last_good = detect.get("last_good_sha")
    bad = (detect.get("bad_shas") or [None])[0]
    if last_good and bad:
        rev = f"{last_good}..{bad}"
    else:
        rev = "-n"
    if rev == "-n":
        log = git("log", "-n", "20", "--format=%H%x09%s", "--", "patient/")
    else:
        log = git("log", "--format=%H%x09%s", rev, "--", "patient/")
    rows = []
    for line in log.splitlines():
        if "\t" not in line:
            continue
        sha, subject = line.split("\t", 1)
        stat = git("show", "--stat", "--format=", sha, "--", "patient/")
        diff = git("show", "--format=", sha, "--", "patient/")
        rows.append({"sha": sha, "subject": subject, "stat": stat, "diff": diff[:8000]})
    return rows


def _overlap(diff: str, hints: str) -> float:
    score = 0.0
    lowered = f"{diff}\n{hints}".lower()
    for token in ("refund", "policy", "config", "inventory", "escalat", "history", "prompt", "paise"):
        if token in diff.lower() and token in lowered:
            score += 0.1
    return score


@neatlogs.span(kind="AGENT", name="locate")
def run(state: dict) -> dict:
    signature = state["outputs"]["DETECT"].get("failure_signature") or ""
    graph_text = ""
    graph_error = None
    try:
        graph_text = call_external(state, "LOCATE", lambda: graph_search(signature))
    except Exception as exc:
        graph_error = str(exc)
    candidates = call_external(state, "LOCATE", lambda: _candidates(state))
    for row in candidates:
        row["overlap"] = _overlap(row["diff"], f"{graph_text}\n{signature}")
    ranking = []
    try:
        packed = [{"sha": row["sha"], "subject": row["subject"], "diff": row["diff"][:2500]} for row in candidates[:8]]
        raw = complete(
            read_prompt("rank.md"),
            f"Failure signature:\n{signature}\n\nCommits:\n{json.dumps(packed)}",
        )
        ranking = parse_json(raw).get("ranking") or []
    except Exception as exc:
        state["errors"].append({"step": "LOCATE", "error": f"rank: {exc}", "at": state.get("updated_at")})
    by_sha = {row["sha"]: row for row in candidates}
    ordered = []
    for item in ranking:
        sha = item.get("sha")
        if sha in by_sha and sha not in {row["sha"] for row in ordered}:
            chosen = dict(by_sha[sha])
            chosen["reason"] = item.get("reason") or ""
            chosen["score"] = float(item.get("score") or chosen["overlap"])
            ordered.append(chosen)
    if not ordered:
        ordered = sorted(candidates, key=lambda row: row["overlap"], reverse=True)
        for row in ordered:
            row["reason"] = "ranked by overlap with the failure signature"
            row["score"] = row["overlap"]
    top = []
    for row in ordered[:3]:
        top.append(
            {
                "sha": row["sha"],
                "subject": row["subject"],
                "reason": row.get("reason", ""),
                "score": row.get("score", 0),
                "stat": row.get("stat", ""),
                "diff": row.get("diff", ""),
            }
        )
    return {"candidates": top, "graph": graph_text[:8000], "graph_error": graph_error}

# Medic

I built Medic because agents rarely crash. They quietly start failing, and
nobody notices until a customer does.

Medic reads a failing agent's trace, finds the broken step, patches one config
file, runs the agent again, and proves the fix with hard checks, including on
tasks it has never seen. The model proposes. The checks decide.

Built for neatHack 2026 by **cipoklean**.

---

## 60-second quickstart

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt

cp .env.example .env          # add NEATLOGS_API_KEY and an LLM key
set -a && . ./.env && set +a  # so .env wins over any stale LLM_* in your shell

.venv/bin/python cli.py doctor
.venv/bin/python cli.py run  --bug parse_error --llm real
.venv/bin/python cli.py heal --bug parse_error --llm real
```

Or use the wrapper, which loads `.env` and pins the patient to `nova-micro` so
the heal is attributed to the right model:

```bash
bash run.sh before    # the failing run
bash run.sh heal      # diagnose, diff, verify, verdict
```

Without `LLM_MODEL_LITELLM_PATIENT` set, the patient falls back to the role
default (`nova-lite`) and Medic also runs on `nova-lite` rather than Sonnet. The
heal still works, but the costs below are measured with the patient pinned.

You will see a red failing run, a diagnosis naming the broken span, a one-line
diff, a green re-run, a held-out results table, and the cost of the repair.

The suites need no key and no network:

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/ -q
```

No Streamlit. No web server. The agent's tools never touch the network.

**The scripted path cannot heal.** `--llm scripted` works for `run`, `report` and
`reset`, but not for `heal`. Medic's diagnose and surgeon steps always use the
real LLM, because a scripted model diagnosing a scripted patient would be
grading its own homework. With no key set, `heal` fails loudly and names the
missing variables.

## How a heal works

```
failing trace -> diagnose -> surgeon -> patch medic.yaml -> verify
  (neatlogs)     real LLM    real LLM     ONE file         train + held-out
                                            never Python   hard checks, no LLM
```

1. **Reproduce.** Run the patient on the buggy config. A deterministic check
   decides whether it actually failed. No LLM opinion involved.
2. **Diagnose.** Send the span tree and the failing check to the LLM. It returns
   a structured diagnosis with a named span and a confidence score.
3. **Patch.** The surgeon writes a patch to `medic.yaml` only. The patch goes to
   a copy and reaches the real file only with `--apply`.
4. **Verify.** Re-run the train task, then every held-out task. All of them must
   pass, or the attempt is rejected and Medic tries again, up to three times.

**Medic edits exactly one file: `medic.yaml`.** Never Python.

| Field | Typical fix |
|---|---|
| `system_prompt` | restore a stop rule, require fetched evidence |
| `tools.<name>.description` | state the argument format with an example |
| `max_steps` | cap a runaway loop |

# Sealed eval, 11 October 2026

Five regressions were planted in the refund agent's history by a second coding session, through ordinary requests to fresh coding sessions. It wrote the answer key, and the key's SHA-256 was committed in 4c45f7f before Whodunit ran on any case. `eval/score.py` checks the key against that hash before scoring. The key was added to git only after every case had been run.

Replays ran on the hackathon gateway's small model, three at a time.

## Result

With 120 replays allowed per case: 3 of 5 solved, 0 wrong accusations, 2 cases where nobody was named.

The two open cases were then resumed from their own replays with up to 200 more allowed: 5 of 5 solved, 0 wrong accusations.

| Case | Rate the second session measured | Rate Whodunit estimated | At 120 replays | In the end | Replays | Commits replayed | Suspects |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| cents-off | 100% | 93% | solved | solved | 21 | 5 | 13 |
| wrong-order-refunded | 30% | 12% | nobody named | solved | 168 | 9 | 12 |
| half-done-batch | 25% | 14% | nobody named | solved | 168 | 10 | 15 |
| strangers-paid | 72% | 59% | solved | solved | 30 | 5 | 11 |
| turned-away | 100% | 93% | solved | solved | 24 | 6 | 14 |

The rate Whodunit estimates is a posterior mean, so after only a few replays it sits below 100% even for a bug that fails every time.

## What it cost

Replay spend on the gateway, estimated from token counts at list prices, came to about $1.91 for all five cases:

- cents-off: about $0.08 (61,267 tokens)
- wrong-order-refunded: about $0.57 (438,034 tokens)
- half-done-batch: about $1.04 (795,110 tokens)
- strangers-paid: about $0.10 (78,530 tokens)
- turned-away: about $0.12 (100,111 tokens)

## What this does and does not show

- No commit was wrongly accused, at either budget. On `half-done-batch` the top suspect at 120 replays was the wrong commit, at 53%, and Whodunit named nobody. That is the behaviour the 95% bar is for.
- The two cases it could not close at 120 replays are the two that fail least often. Whodunit put them at 12% and 14%, where the second session had measured 30% and 25% from a handful of probes. A bug that rare needs a lot of replays whatever the method.
- The ranges are short, 11 to 15 suspects. On ranges this size a careful scan from the oldest commit would have replayed about as many commits as Whodunit did, so this eval says little about savings on long histories. The simulator in `eval/simulator` covers 40 suspects.
- Five cases is a small sample. It is enough to say the pipeline works on a history it did not write, and not enough to put a number on accuracy.
- Each case has one planted regression inside its range, by design. Two regressions that touch the same inputs in one range are outside what the model assumes.

# Simulator results

How often does the lineup name the right commit, for a given number of replays? This folder answers that with simulated cases, where the culprit is known.

Each case has 40 suspect commits and one culprit picked at random. Every point is 500 cases. Three methods get the same cases and the same replay budget:

- The statistical bisect in `whodunit/lineup.py`. It names a commit only when it is 95% sure, and otherwise hands back the suspects that remain with their probabilities.
- Plain bisect with repeats. It replays each commit as many times as the budget allows and calls the commit bad on the first failure.
- Plain bisect with one replay per commit, which is what `git bisect run` does.

To regenerate everything here, run `uv run python -m whodunit.simulate --out eval/simulator`. It takes about two minutes. `tables.md` has every number behind the charts, and `results.json` has the raw counts.

## When good commits never fail

![Accuracy against replay budget when good commits never fail](accuracy-clean-baseline.svg)

Plain bisect with repeats wins here at every budget. For a bug that fails 30% of the time, 80 replays get it to 97% while the statistical bisect names the right commit in 67% of cases. The statistical bisect needs 160 replays to reach 93%.

The reason is that plain bisect with repeats assumes a single failure convicts a commit, and in this world that is true. The statistical bisect does not assume it. It starts out believing a good commit fails about 5% of the time and spends replays finding out.

Two things are worth knowing before picking plain bisect on that basis. Its mistakes are silent: with 40 replays on the 30% bug it names the wrong commit in 26% of cases and gives no sign of it, where the statistical bisect names the wrong one in 2% and says "not sure yet" in the rest. And the dashed line shows the statistical bisect's top suspect is right in 91% of cases at 80 replays, so most of its "not sure yet" answers are pointing at the culprit already.

Plain bisect with one replay per commit is right 10% of the time on the 30% bug, at any budget.

## When good commits fail 5% of the time on their own

![Accuracy against replay budget when good commits fail 5% of the time](accuracy-flaky-baseline.svg)

Agents are rarely this clean. Give every good commit a 5% chance of failing by itself and plain bisect with repeats falls apart, and more replays make it worse. On the 30% bug it is right in 31% of cases with 40 replays and 4% with 320, because every extra replay of an innocent commit is another chance for a stray failure 
# Whodunit

41 commits since it last worked. Which one did it?

Whodunit answers two questions about an AI agent that used to work and now fails: which commit broke it, and why that commit was made. Then it fixes the commit, proves the fix by replaying the failures, and counts what the breakage cost.

It was built for neatHack between 10 and 12 October 2026. `hackathon.md` is the dated build log, including the parts that went wrong.

## Why plain bisect is not enough

`git bisect` assumes a bad commit fails every time. Agents do not behave that way. A prompt change might break one run in three, and a commit that is perfectly fine might still fail one run in twenty. Test a bad commit once, see it pass, and bisect walks off in the wrong direction without telling yo

Whodunit replays the failing inputs against suspect commits and keeps a probability for each suspect being the first bad one. It names a commit only when it is 95% sure. If the replay budget runs out first, it hands back the suspects still in the lineup with their probabilities.

How well that works is measured two ways. [eval/sealed](eval/sealed/README.md) is five regressions planted by a separate session with a sealed answer key: three were named inside 120 replays, all five after more, and no commit was wrongly accused. [eval/simulator](eval/simulator/README.md) is simula

## How a case runs

A case is a small TOML file: a symptom, the failing inputs with what each should have produced, the last good ref and the first bad ref.

```bash
uv run whodunit lineup cases/my-case.toml      # replay against the suspects and name the culprit
uv run whodunit brief cases/my-case.toml       # what the commit was asked to do, and a root-cause brief
uv run whodunit ruling cases/my-case.toml      # one question for the owner: revert, or keep the intent and patch
uv run whodunit fix cases/my-case.toml         # apply it on a branch and replay until the fix is proven
uv run whodunit damages cases/my-case.toml     # bad runs and what they cost
uv run whodunit open-case cases/my-case.toml   # the case file, as one HTML page
```

Each step adds to one record next to the case file, and the case file page is drawn from that record.

1. The lineup checks every suspect commit out into its own git worktree and replays the case inputs there. Each replay is a real run of the agent, traced to neatroots and tagged with the commit and the case. A commit that will not build is skipped, as `git bisect skip` does.
2. The motive comes from Entire. A commit made by a coding agent carries a checkpoint, and the checkpoint holds the session. Whodunit finds the prompt that led to the commit and what the coding agent did next.
3. The brief is written by a model from the culprit's diff, that slice of the session, and a failing run set against a passing one. Every sentence has to cite a span, a commit or a checkpoint that is really in the evidence. Sentences that do not are cut.
4. The ruling is the owner's. It is asked once per kind of change (a prompt change, a tool change, a dependency) and remembered under `rulings/`.
5. The fix is a revert or a patch on a local branch. It is replayed until it is 95% likely fixed or 95% likely not, and the case is kept under `cases/` as a regression test that `whodunit check` can replay against any ref.
6. The damages are counted from the traces: how many runs went bad since the failures began, and an estimate of what they cost.

Whodunit never pushes, opens a pull request or writes to anyone's finance model by itself. Those stay with the owner.

# Autopsy — a debugger for AI-agent mistakes

**Team Last Commit · [neatHack 2026](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon)**

Autopsy investigates *why* an AI-agent run failed — not just *where*. It is
itself an agent: given a failing run, it combines three evidence sources

- **neatlogs traces** — what the failing agent actually did at runtime
  (every LLM call, tool call, input, output, error)
- **Entire checkpoints** — which coding-agent session produced each commit,
  with the transcript of what it was asked to do
- **Entire graph** — semantic code search and entity-level per-commit changes

and emits an evidence-backed diagnosis: root cause, the exact trace step
where it surfaced, the culprit commit **and the session transcript behind
it**, plus a suggested fix.

The debugger's own investigation is fully traced in neatlogs too — the tool
for debugging agents is itself an observable agent.

## Why this matters

When an agent misbehaves, today's tools show you the *what* (a bad answer, a
failed tool call) but not the *why*. The why usually lives in two places at
once: the runtime evidence (the trace) and the development history (who
changed what, and what they were trying to do). Autopsy is the first tool
that joins those two timelines: trace span → suspect code → the checkpoint
and coding-agent transcript that introduced it.

## Demo result (live, reproducible)

We broke a small research agent (`demo_agent`) on purpose: a debugging
session flipped `search_docs` from descending to ascending order, so the
search tool started returning the *least* relevant pages first. The agent's
answer degraded — it could no longer describe the flag of Azerbaijan.

Autopsy's diagnosis on the failing trace, verbatim:

> **Root cause:** `search_docs` sorts ascending (`reverse=False` at
> `demo_agent/app.py:51`), so worst matches come first and the
> `flag-of-azerbaijan` page is cut before it reaches the LLM.
> **Failing step:** all four `search_docs` calls returned the same three
> lowest-scoring pages regardless of query phrasing.
> **Culprit:** checkpoint `01M4K1P5A9NYJJNRY2D9XKJ08P` — commit
> `dece484` "Flip search_docs ordering for ranking inspection".
> **Fix:** `reverse=True`.

After the fix commit, the same question produces the full correct answer
(*"horizontal tricolour of blue, red, and green, with a white crescent and
an eight-pointed star"*).

| Artifact | Link / ID |
|---|---|
| Culprit commit + sessions (Entire) | [dece484 on Entire](https://entire.io/gh/FaridMahmudlu/neathack-agent/commit/dece4846baaed3c5961447af4c0d99a7dd273ed1) |
| Checkpoint — benign change | `01M4K1KECVQ0VNT4GVGB9KCB90` (`f4df4da`) |
| Checkpoint — bug introduced | `01M4K1P5A9NYJJNRY2D9XKJ08P` (`dece484`) |
| Checkpoint — fix | `01M4K1V2G1WYATMGMNK0ZP2KQH` (`63e69d5`) |
| neatlogs trace — bugged run | `98330b2d046133fee546ecfc1c011915` |
| neatlogs trace — Autopsy's own investigation | `62c2dce9659d83e26711fe123e8c3dc7` |
| neatlogs trace — verified fixed run | `ead5a98e094a5e2495f6e428c41fc196` |

A nice side-effect captured by the checkpoints: the coding agent (OpenCode +
Claude Haiku) was asked twice to introduce the regression as a "refactor"
and *refused* — it negated the score instead of flipping the order,
preserving correct behaviour. The bug only landed when asked as a debugging
experiment. The transcripts tell that whole story; Autopsy reads them.

## What I could and couldn't see

- **GitHub:** about 120 public repos mention the hackathon. Roughly 80 have real work and 25 are a README or less. I read the README, file list and commit log for each, plus the code of the closest rivals.
- **X:** search needs a sign-in, so I only saw the posts that repos link to (12 links across 5 repos). Post counts below are a floor.
- **Not checked:** I did not open live sites, videos, trace links or cfo.ai links, so "has a link" means the README shows one.

## The same idea as ours

Three entries ask "which commit broke the agent, and why was it written".

| Entry | How it finds the culprit | Tools shown | How far along |
|---|---|---|---|
| [AgentBisect](https://github.com/jaxsonsprinkles/agentbisect) | Worktree replays, then pass-rate thresholds (85% or more is good, 50% or less is bad, anything between is "flaky") | neatlogs CLI intake, Entire checkpoints on 3 of 4 commits, no cfo.ai | Scaffold. Bisect not built, no live model run, target history not grown. Started at 11:42 PM Saturday and moving fast |
| [Autopsy](https://github.com/FaridMahmudlu/neathack-agent) | A model with 14 tools reads the trace and checkpoints. No replay across commits | Three trace ids, a checkpoint link, a cfo.ai plan with a share link | Two planted bugs diagnosed in a 24-commit repo. Narration audio recorded, video in production |
| [Rootline](https://github.com/bruce249/rootline) | A model ranks the diffs of the top 8 commits | Entire runners and graph config, neatlogs wired, cfo.ai inputs only | 4 commits, baseline only, quiet since 9 PM Saturday |

All three use planted bugs that fail every time. A bug that fails 30% of the time gives a 70% pass rate, which lands in AgentBisect's "flaky" band, and the other two never replay at all.

## Repairing a failing agent from its traces

This is the most crowded idea. None of these asks which commit caused the failure.

| Entry | Tools shown | How far along |
|---|---|---|
| [Mend](https://github.com/thegoodengineers/mend) | Trace files, 4 detections, a checkpoint link, a cfo.ai export (xlsx) | 72 commits, website, 2-minute demo video, held-out test, a "for judges: 60 seconds" table, one post |
| [Pitstop](https://github.com/ROHITCRAFTSYT/pitstop) | 9 traces read back, 7 entire-graph searches | 0 of 6 to 6 of 6 tasks, tokens down 72%, one post |
| [Medic](https://github.com/cipoklean/medic) | Checkpoint link, cfo.ai input docs | 70 commits, one real repair at $0.009, held-out checks |
| [Suture](https://github.com/Sireadell/suture) | neatlogs read through the CLI, 14 checkpoints | One proven target, a pull request opened |
| [VeriFix](https://github.com/shivanshjain456/neatHack) | Claims everything: 11 detections, Graph, Brain, Trails, all 8 of Entire's suggested ideas, cfo.ai workbook | Live page, 2:50 video, a 36 KB README with claims like "488x cheaper" |

## The front-runners on evidence

| Entry | What it does | Why it is ahead |
|---|---|---|
| [FirstRun](https://github.com/HighnessAtharva/firstrun) | Runs a docs quickstart in a clean container, fixes the broken step, proves it | The current leader: 114 commits, live site, launch film, 4 upstream PRs (one to Entire's own CLI), public cfo.ai model, neatlogs detections with screenshots, Entire Trails and Brain, 5 or more posts |
| [Crashtest](https://github.com/emreozyoruk/crashtest) | Maps a repo into user scenarios and runs them | Real bugs in three public apps, including neatroots at a neatlogs staffer's request, plus three cfo.ai share links |
| [Cair](https://github.com/edycutjong/cair) | Plans prize payouts to non-US bank accounts | Live app, neatlogs screenshots, public cfo.ai model, two posts, no checkpoints |
| [hioffer](https://github.com/haodaz/hioffer) | PhD application agent | All three tools shown with artefacts, 43 of 45 commits with checkpoints, live site |
| [migration-parachute](https://github.com/Sher110106/migration-parachute) | Safe Postgres migrations | Clean before and after table, entire-graph output, demo video |
| [Spend Radar](https://github.com/akarsh-dhingra/SpeedRadar-NeetHack) | Compares people spend with competitors | 37 checkpoints, cfo.ai scenarios, held-out scorecards |

[Roster](https://github.com/rajkaria/roster) (165 commits, 81 checkpoints) reviews coding-agent sessions recorded by Entire, but its results file still says "PENDING". About 50 repos have a business plan file, 10 link a checkpoint, 6 have a video, and 5 link posts.
